name_ru: Тун Му Чжэн Шань Сяо Чжун
processing: Fully oxidised black tea; the traditional version is dried over burning pine, which supplied warmth in the cool, high valley and leaves a smoky aroma. Unsmoked versions are also made.
harvest_season: Spring is usual for the better lots, as with most Wuyi black teas.
appearance_dry: Tight, even strips, iron-dark with a brownish, slightly oily sheen.
taste_profile: Mellow and clearly sweet, with a longan-like richness; smoked versions carry pine smoke woven into that sweetness rather than sitting on top of it.

brewing.notes: Short steeps in a gaiwan keep it sweet. It also takes milk well in a Western pot.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, usually the current or previous spring, in smoked and unsmoked versions that should be labelled as such. Real Tongmu leaf is scarce and much sold under the name is not from there, so the village and maker matter more than the label. It keeps a few years if dry and sealed.
description:
This is Lapsang Souchong from its home ground: the Tongmu area in the Wuyi Mountains nature reserve in northern Fujian. The name separates it from 'outside mountain' teas (waishan xiaozhong), which are copies made elsewhere, often from gongfu black tea smoked afterwards.

The valley is high and cool, which is the usual explanation for the pine: makers burned it to keep oxidation going, and the leaf took up the smoke. Today both smoked and unsmoked versions are made. Only bushes of the local seed-grown Wuyi caicha within the protected area are supposed to qualify under current origin rules.

A good cup is deep amber and sweet first, with a longan-like richness and, in smoked lots, a pine note that stays calm. Harsh tar or ash points to heavy smoking of weak leaf. Keep steeps short; it also holds up to milk.

When buying, ask whether it is smoked, which year and which village. Genuine Tongmu tea is a small share of what carries the name, so a very low price is a warning.
history:
Accounts usually place the start of small-leaf black tea here in the late Ming, though the often-quoted '400 years' comes mainly from trade and promotional writing rather than close historical study. The tea moved through the market town of Xingcun, which gave it the alternative name Xingcun Xiaozhong.

The word 'zhengshan', suggesting the true or proper mountain, is often explained by competition between genuine and outside teas after the Opium Wars. Later, gongfu black teas developed from this style, and Jin Jun Mei was developed from its methods in this century.
